models.summary: Health is split into performance and potential, and each gets its own indicator set and its own IEW-TOPSIS run. System A: coverage, fairness, achievement, 10 positive indicators. System B: input, output, efficiency, 11 indicators, of which the student-teacher ratio is negative. Entropy weights, then closeness to the ideal. Equal-interval grades: poor below 0.25, fair below 0.5, good below 0.75, excellent above. On performance, 11 countries exceed 0.5 and only 2 exceed 0.6; Slovak Republic 0.639816, Israel 0.264504. Chile scores 0.279497 on performance and 0.73439 on potential, the widest gap, and is the case.
models.purpose: Rank countries twice, once on current benefit to youth and once on room to improve, so the case is the country worst on the first and best on the second.
objectives: Turn two qualitative evaluation systems into scores that can be compared across 21 countries.

equation_status.note: Every formula on pages 12 and 13 is printed with private-use glyphs, so the algebra is reconstructed as standard IEW-TOPSIS. The reported scores are readable.
equation_status.reason: Steps are numbered and the outputs are tabulated.

details: 21 OECD countries, data for 2016, from OECD reports and databases. Missing values borrowed from within two years of the base year.
System A has 10 indicators, all positive. System B has 11, one negative. Coverage is treated as the base of fairness, and fairness as the base of achievement.

parameter_estimation.method: Entropy weights computed separately inside each system. No subjective weights.

algorithm.description: Standardize, compute entropy weights, vector-normalize, measure weighted distances to the best and worst rows, convert to closeness, grade and rank.
algorithm.convergence_criteria: Not applicable. The score is a closed computation.

details: Slovak Republic 0.639816, Israel 0.264504 on performance. Chile 0.279497 and 0.73439. After the vision is substituted, Chile's performance rises to 0.444658.
identifiability_feasibility.analysis: The two rankings disagree, which is the point. A single index would have hidden Chile's combination of a bad present and a large ceiling.

constraints: Two separate runs, weights not shared.
strengths: Refusing AHP is argued from a named defect, reliance on one supervisor.
The scatter of the two scores is used as a check on the split itself.
limitations: The entropy story is told backwards: high entropy is said to mean less change, then used as a reason for weight.
No weight table is printed, so the ranking cannot be recomputed from the text.
missing_details: Which countries form the ten below 0.5 on performance.
assumptions: Quantity can compensate a moderate quality gap.
Unfairness comes from income and status.
Public institutions pursue justice and private ones efficiency.
No shocks, and slow change without a strong policy.

models.summary: Chile's master-to-undergraduate ratio, the youngest in the sample, is forecast with GM(1,1) on Ministry of Education data from 2007 to 2018, after a level-ratio deviation test. From 2016 to 2028 the ratio rises only about 46 percent. That misses the vision, so a strong policy is called imperative. The same device later substitutes the vision values back into TOPSIS: Chile's performance moves from 0.279497 to 0.444658, still only fair, and the authors say the policy is not sufficient.
models.purpose: Show that the chosen indicator will not reach its target on its own, and then show that even the target leaves the system short of healthy.
objectives: Forecast twelve years of one ratio and compare the endpoint with the vision.

governing_equations.source_expression: yh_t = (y_1 - b_g/a_g) exp(-a_g (t-1)) + b_g/a_g, then first difference restored
governing_equations.purpose: Standard GM(1,1). The printed equation is not legible; the model name, the test, and the 46 percent result are.

equation_status.note: No clean equation is printed. The model is named GM(1,1), the level-ratio test is said to pass, and the conclusion is a 46 percent rise over 12 years.
equation_status.reason: Named, tested, coded in Python, and plotted as Figure 11.

details: Annual ratio, 2007-2018, Chilean Ministry of Education. OECD and national calibers differ; the trend is assumed similar.
Forecast 2019-2028. Target is the 21-country mean of the ratio, 0.363, against Chile's 0.115.

parameter_estimation.method: Least squares on the accumulated series, as usual for GM(1,1). The estimated a and b are not reported. A level-ratio deviation test is said to pass.

algorithm.description: Test the level ratio, fit GM(1,1), forecast to 2028, compare with the mean target.
algorithm.convergence_criteria: Level-ratio deviation test passed. No error number is given.

details: About 46 percent growth in twelve years, from the youngest starting point in the sample. Not enough to reach 0.363.
identifiability_feasibility.analysis: The forecast does the job it was given, which is to fail. Its parameters and errors are not shown, so the size of the miss is not checkable.

strengths: The forecast is used before the policy, as a reason for acting, not as a decoration after it.
Three reasons for the grey model are stated: few data, grey causality, testable.
limitations: No parameters, no fitted values, no residual.
The authors later concede the predicted series is not smooth enough and the error may be large.
assumptions: Different statistical calibers share a trend.
Without a strong policy, change stays slow.
